seriesSubtitle: Single Men's Group · Biblically Based · 10-Week Expanded Curriculum
accountabilityQuestions: Where did you win spiritually this week?
Where did you struggle or fall short?
Did you do what you said you'd do last week?
Is there anything you're not telling us?

weeks.title: You Are the Beloved
weeks.subtitle: Identity, Singleness & Finding God's Love When You Are Alone
weeks.bigIdea: The most important truth a single man can know is not "God has a plan for my life" — it is "I am loved by God right now, before I accomplish anything, before I find anyone, exactly as I am." Until that is more than a doctrine — until it is a lived reality — everything else in this curriculum is built on sand.
weeks.coreTension: Single men often experience their singleness as evidence of being unchosen — and unchosen as unloved. This session names that lie and offers the only foundation that actually holds.
weeks.opening: Ask the group to introduce themselves without using their job title or relationship status: "Who are you? You can't say what you do for work or whether you're in a relationship." Let the silence happen. After everyone has gone: "Most of us don't know how to answer that without our accomplishments or our roles. Tonight we're going to look at what God says about who you are before you do anything."

teaching.title: I. Made and Declared Significant — Genesis 1:26–27

scriptures.text: "Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness...So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him.'"

prose: The word image (tselem) was used in the ancient world to describe a statue placed in a territory to represent a king's authority. You are not just a creature — you are God's representative. This declaration was made before any command, before any work. You are significant before you produce anything. Your singleness does not reduce your image-bearing.

teaching.title: II. Fully Known and Not Hidden — Psalm 139:13–16

scriptures.text: "For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made...My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret..."

prose: Many single men live with a gnawing sense of invisibility. The world's romantic economy says: if no one has chosen you, you are less visible, less valuable. Psalm 139 answers: you are not invisible. You are seen completely and have been since before you were born. Fearfully — the Hebrew means with reverence and awe.

teaching.title: III. Adopted, Not Just Forgiven — Romans 8:14–17

scriptures.text: "You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'"

prose: Forgiveness restores a broken relationship. Adoption creates a new one. Many men understand they are forgiven but don't live like they are sons. Abba — the Aramaic word a child uses for their father. Intimate, informal, like "Dad." The spirit of slavery = performance, striving, fear. The spirit of adoption = belonging, security, access.

teaching.title: IV. You Are the Beloved — Abba's Child, Chapter 4

scriptures.text: "Define yourself radically as one beloved by God. This is the true self. Every other identity is illusion." — Brennan Manning

prose: Manning centers Chapter 4 on Jesus' baptism in Luke 3:22 — before Jesus performed one miracle or preached one sermon, the Father declared: "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased." The love was not a reward for ministry. It was the foundation for it.

For single men specifically: the ache of being without a spouse is real. But no human love — not a wife, not success — can fill the place that only Abba's love was designed to fill. A man who has not found his belovedness in God will demand it from a woman, and that demand will crush both of them.

teaching.title: V. Singleness Is Not a Waiting Room — Not Yet Married
prose: Segal: "What if singleness is not the absence of something, but the presence of something?" Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:32–35 describes singleness as a season of undivided devotion to God — not a punishment, not a holding pattern, but a unique capacity for focus that marriage actually reduces.

"The man who is unsatisfied in God will be unsatisfied in marriage. The man who finds his satisfaction in God will bring something real to a marriage rather than demanding that his wife be something she was never meant to be."

scriptureRefs.text: "Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness...So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him.'"

"For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made...My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret..."
"You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'"

discussionQuestions: Without using your job or relationship status — who are you? What came up when you tried to answer that at the start of tonight?
Manning says: "Define yourself radically as one beloved by God." What would actually change in your daily life if you believed that without qualification?
Is it easier for you to believe God forgave you or that God actually likes you — delights in you? What's the difference, and which one do you live from?
How have you been experiencing your singleness — as a waiting room, a deficiency, a failure, or something else?
Segal: "The man who is unsatisfied in God will be unsatisfied in marriage." Do you think that's true? What does satisfaction in God look like practically?
weeks.application:
Read Abba's Child, Chapter 4. Every morning, read Luke 3:22 and say out loud: "I am the beloved." It will feel strange. Do it anyway — seven days in a row.
Write down three lies you believe about yourself because of your singleness. Next to each one, write what God actually says. Bring one to share next week.
reading: Not Yet Married Introduction & Ch. 1 — Segal

weeks.title: The Impostor & the Inner Life
weeks.subtitle: The False Self, Spiritual Disciplines & Becoming Who You Actually Are
weeks.bigIdea: Every man builds a false self — a managed, performed version designed to earn approval and avoid rejection. Spiritual formation is the lifelong process of dismantling the Impostor. The hidden habits of prayer, Scripture, and fasting are the training ground.
weeks.coreTension: Men are more comfortable with external performance than internal formation. The Impostor loves religious activity because it can be performed publicly. Real formation happens in private, where the Impostor has nothing to work with.

teaching.title: I. The Impostor — Abba's Child, Chapter 2

scriptures.text: "The impostor is not the real me and, therefore, cannot have a true relationship with God. A false self cannot have a real encounter with the God who is real." — Manning

prose: Manning names the mechanism behind every man's hidden life: the Impostor is the false self every man constructs to manage how others see him. He was built for survival — at some point, showing the real you felt too dangerous. So you built a representative.

Signs the Impostor is running your life: You spend significant energy managing what others think. You feel relief when sessions like this end without anyone getting too close. You have different "modes" — church mode, work mode, friend mode — and none of them are quite you.

teaching.title: II. Guard Your Heart Above All Else — Proverbs 4:23

scriptures.text: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life."

prose: The word keep (natsar) is a military word — guard, protect, watch. The Impostor guards the heart from harm but also seals it off from life. Nothing real gets in. Nothing real gets out. Guarding your heart in a godly way means being deliberate about what you allow to shape you, while remaining genuinely open to God and trusted others.

teaching.title: III. The Disciplines Are the Training Ground — 1 Timothy 4:7–8

scriptures.text: "Rather train yourself for godliness; for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way."

prose: The Greek word for train is gymnazo — athletic language. Jesus began His public ministry with 40 days of fasting and solitude (Luke 4:1–2). His spiritual reserves were full because of prior discipline. The disciplines — Scripture, prayer, fasting, solitude — form the real self and starve the Impostor. The Impostor cannot fast because fasting is done in secret with no audience to perform for.

teaching.title: IV. The Blessed Man Lives From the Inside Out — Psalm 1

scriptures.text: "His delight is in the law of the LORD...He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season."

prose: The blessed man is described by what he delights in — not just what he does. The Impostor can perform duty; he cannot manufacture genuine delight. The tree image: a tree near a stream doesn't strain for water — it is simply positioned correctly. The disciplines are not ways to earn God's favor; they are ways of positioning yourself near the stream.

scriptureRefs.text: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life."
"Rather train yourself for godliness; for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way."
"His delight is in the law of the LORD...He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season."

discussionQuestions: Manning describes the Impostor as the false self you send out to manage others' perceptions. Do you recognize yours? What does he perform, hide, or project?
Manning says: "A false self cannot have a real encounter with the God who is real." What would that mean for your prayer life if the person showing up to pray is the Impostor?
What does your current routine with God actually look like — be honest, not aspirational?
Singleness gives you time for spiritual formation that marriage reduces. Are you investing that time, or waiting until "later" to get serious about your inner life?
What's one area of private life you would be uncomfortable with God — or this group — seeing? Acknowledge whether it exists, even if you don't name it specifically.
weeks.application:
Read Abba's Child, Chapter 2. Commit to a 7-day Scripture plan — bring back one observation (not necessarily profound; just whether you showed up). Skip one meal and use that time to pray. When the Impostor tries to perform the prayer, stop and start again honestly.
Tonight: Pair off into accountability partners. Exchange numbers. Agree on one mid-week check-in question.

weeks.title: Father Wounds & The Father's Voice
weeks.subtitle: Healing, Hearing from Abba, and What You Needed
weeks.bigIdea: Many men cannot receive God's love as Abba because their earthly father left no safe template for it. Until the wound is named, it shapes everything — how you see God, how you relate to women, and how you lead. God isn't patching a broken father image. He's replacing it.
weeks.coreTension: Weeks 1 and 2 asked men to receive Abba's love. This week confronts what blocks that reception: the gap between the father you needed and the father you got. You cannot receive from Abba what your earthly father failed to model until you name what was missing.
weeks.opening: Say directly: "Last week we talked about the Impostor — the false self built to manage how others see us. This week we're going underneath that to ask: where did that Impostor come from? For most men, the answer begins with their father." Then share one honest piece of your own story with your father — not cleaned up, not resolved. Real.

teaching.title: I. The Father We Needed — Isaiah 49:15–16

scriptures.text: "Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands."

prose: God speaks here as a parent who remembers even when parents fail. "Engraved on the palms of my hands" — permanent, intentional, costly. Some of the men in this room had fathers who forgot them through absence, addiction, anger, or neglect. God makes a direct promise: even if they forget, I will not.

teaching.title: II. The Father Running — Luke 15:11–24

scriptures.text: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

prose: The father in this parable does three things no Jewish patriarch in Jesus' culture would do: he sees his son from a distance (meaning he was watching for him), he runs (undignified for an elderly man of his station), and he embraces him before the son can deliver his prepared speech. This is a portrait of God's posture toward you — not waiting for you to get your act together, but running toward you while you are still a long way off.

Manning writes extensively about this scene in Abba's Child. The question he asks: can you let the Father run toward you? Or do you stop him with a prepared speech — "I am no more worthy to be called your son" — before he can get to you?

teaching.title: III. When the Father Forsakes — Psalm 27:10

scriptures.text: "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in."

prose: David writes this from experience. This is not a hypothetical: "even if" your father abandoned you. It is written as if that already happened. And the response is not denial — it is redirection. The Lord receives me. The Hebrew word for take me in is the same used for gathering the abandoned or the homeless into shelter. God is not a replacement father in a thin sense. He is the true Father who does not abandon.

teaching.title: IV. Rooted in the Father's Love — Ephesians 3:14–19

scriptures.text: "That you, being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge."

prose: Paul prays for men to be rooted and grounded in love — both images suggest something anchored, structural, beneath the surface. A man rooted in the Father's love is not easily uprooted by the next woman's approval or disapproval, not destabilized by singleness, not driven by the fear that he is not enough. That root system takes time to grow — but it begins by naming what was missing and turning toward the One who is not missing.

scriptureRefs.text: "Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands."
"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."
"For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in."

"That you, being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge."

discussionQuestions: What did your father teach you about your worth — through presence, absence, or both? What was the loudest message, spoken or unspoken?
Is "Abba Father" warm or complicated for you right now? You don't have to defend the answer — just say what's true.
How has your father's example shaped how you imagine God's posture toward you — distant, critical, passive, present?
What is one thing you needed from your father that you didn't receive? Have you ever named it out loud — to anyone?
The prodigal's father ran toward him before the son could give his speech. Is there a part of you that keeps God at arm's length with a prepared performance? What is the speech?
weeks.application:
Read Luke 15:11–24 every morning this week. Read it as a portrait of how God sees you, not just as a parable about prodigals.
Write two things: one thing your father gave you (even if imperfect) and one thing he couldn't give you. Bring one to share next week. You don't have to share both — but bring one.
reading: Abba's Child Ch. 1 & 7 — father wounds and Abba's embrace — Manning

weeks.title: Sexuality & Purity
weeks.subtitle: God's Design, the Honest Conversation, and the Gospel Response
weeks.bigIdea: Sexual struggle for a single man is directly connected to the loneliness and longing named in Weeks 1–3. A man who does not know he is loved by God will use sexual sin to feel desired, wanted, and temporarily less alone. The gospel — not shame, not willpower — is the only thing that actually addresses the root.
weeks.coreTension: Leader Note: Lead this session with grace, not shame. Set the tone before you begin: "Every man in this room has dealt with this in some form. This is not a room of exceptions." Your own honesty in this session will determine how honest the room gets.

teaching.title: I. God's Design Was Good Before Sin — Genesis 2:18–25

scriptures.text: "A man shall...hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed."

prose: "Naked and not ashamed" — this is the original design. Full vulnerability with no fear, no performance anxiety, no exploitation. Sin did not create sexuality. Sin corrupted it. The one-flesh union images the oneness of the Trinity: complete, mutual, intimate. The answer to corrupted sex is not less sex — it is restored sex within covenant.

teaching.title: II. The Body Is a Temple, Not a Tool — 1 Corinthians 6:18–20

scriptures.text: "Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price."

prose: "You are not your own" — the most countercultural statement in the passage. Your body was purchased. For single men: the loneliness of singleness can make sexual sin feel like it meets a real need. It doesn't. It creates the feeling of connection while replacing the real thing with a counterfeit that leaves you more isolated, not less.

teaching.title: III. Lust Is a Worship Problem — Matthew 5:27–30

scriptures.text: "Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart."

prose: Jesus moves the standard from behavior to the heart. Lust is treating another person as an object for your gratification. At its root, lust is a form of idolatry — reaching for something created to fill the place only the Creator can fill. Pornography specifically: it hijacks the reward system, rewires expectation, dehumanizes, and grows in isolation. Shame drives it underground, where it gets worse.

teaching.title: IV. The Gospel Is Bigger Than Willpower — Romans 6:11–14

scriptures.text: "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God...For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace."

prose: Under law, failure means condemnation. Under grace, failure means returning to the Father and continuing to fight. Flee (2 Tim 2:22) — not "stand your ground and white-knuckle it." Remove the access. The man fighting loneliness only through sexual sin has no replacement for what he is fleeing. The man building genuine connection has something to run toward when temptation comes.

scriptureRefs.text: "A man shall...hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed."
"Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price."
"Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
"So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God...For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace."

discussionQuestions: What messages did you receive growing up about sex — from your family, church, and culture? How have those shaped what you believe now?
If lust is a worship problem rather than a willpower problem, how does that change the way you fight it?
Segal connects sexual sin for single men to loneliness — using sex to feel wanted and less alone. Do you recognize that in your own experience?
What does fleeing (2 Tim 2:22) actually look like in your specific situation?
What would it look like to fight this battle from a place of being known and loved by God rather than from guilt and shame?
weeks.application:
Tonight: Every man installs an accountability app (Covenant Eyes or Accountable2You) and shares access with their accountability partner before leaving. Do it in the room together — don't leave it to individual follow-through. The leader goes first.
This week: Read Not Yet Married chapters on sexuality. Note one specific thing that challenges your current thinking.
reading: Not Yet Married — sexuality and purity chapters — Segal

weeks.title: Loneliness & the Fight for Brotherhood
weeks.subtitle: Being Known vs. Being Near — Building Covenant Friendship
weeks.bigIdea: Loneliness is not the absence of people — it is the absence of being truly known. Single men in their 20s and 30s are statistically the loneliest demographic in the developed world. The gospel offers not just proximity but covenant. And covenant-level friendship requires the same thing intimacy with God requires: the willingness to be seen.
weeks.coreTension: Men can be surrounded by people and still deeply alone. This session bridges the identity work of Weeks 1–4 with the brotherhood work of Week 6 — naming the loneliness honestly before naming the solution.
weeks.opening: Start with a direct question, no warm-up: "How many of you have, at this exact moment, at least one person in your life who knows what's actually going on with you — not just the surface stuff, but the real thing? How many of you could call someone right now, not for logistics, but just to say 'I'm not okay'?" Let the hands (or silence) do the work. Then: "What we're building in this room is trying to be part of the answer to that."

teaching.title: I. Not Good Alone — Genesis 2:18

scriptures.text: "Then the LORD God said, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.'"

prose: This declaration was made in Eden — before sin, before the fall, in the state of original perfection. Adam was in unbroken fellowship with God and still God said: it is not good to be alone. This means human loneliness is not a spiritual failure or a lack of faith. It is a design reality. You were made for both vertical intimacy with God and horizontal intimacy with other humans. Neither replaces the other.

teaching.title: II. The Two-Are-Better Economy — Ecclesiastes 4:9–12

scriptures.text: "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!...A threefold cord is not quickly broken."

prose: "Woe to him who is alone when he falls" — this is compassionate, not judgmental. It is a warning about the danger of isolation. The man without a cord of brotherhood is not less spiritual. He is in a profoundly more vulnerable position. Sin, doubt, depression, and addiction all thrive in isolation and weaken in community.

teaching.title: III. More Than Servants — John 15:13–15

scriptures.text: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you."

prose: Friendship with Jesus is defined by full disclosure. He holds nothing back from his friends. The model for human friendship carries this implication: real friendship requires being known, not just liked. Most men have people who like them — people who enjoy their company, laugh at their jokes, show up to the game. Far fewer have people who know them. The distance between those two things is where loneliness lives.

teaching.title: IV. Stirring One Another — Hebrews 10:24–25

scriptures.text: "And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near."

prose: The word stir up is the Greek paroxysmos — the same word that gives us paroxysm. It means to provoke, to sharpen, to agitate into action. Real brotherhood is not passive. It requires intentional presence — showing up, following up, asking real questions, refusing to let a man drift. The drift is quiet. You don't notice it happening. Which is why the author says: consider how to stir one another. Think about it. Be intentional.

scriptureRefs.text: "Then the LORD God said, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.'"

"Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!...A threefold cord is not quickly broken."
"No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you."

"And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near."

discussionQuestions: Be honest: are you lonely? Not "I could use more friends" — actually lonely in a way you don't often name?
What is the difference between being around people and being genuinely known by them?
Why do you think it's harder for men to pursue deep friendship than to pursue a woman romantically? What does that reveal?
"It is not good for man to be alone" was said in Eden before sin. What does it mean that God built the need for human connection into your design — and what does it mean when you ignore that need?
What would it cost you to let the men in this room actually know you — not the Sunday school version, but the real you?
weeks.application:
Tonight: Every man pulls out his phone and texts one man outside this group before leaving the room. Not "let's hang sometime" — a real question. Something like: "Hey man — how are you actually doing right now?" Do it together, before anyone leaves.
This week: Share something real with your accountability partner that you normally wouldn't say. It doesn't have to be dramatic. Just something true that you usually keep inside.
reading: Not Yet Married — community and singleness chapters — Segal

weeks.title: Brotherhood & Pursuing a Woman Well
weeks.subtitle: Friendship, Integrity-Based Dating & Pursuing From Fullness
weeks.bigIdea: Two of the most important relationships in a single man's life are the friendships that hold him accountable and the woman he pursues with integrity. Both require the same foundation: a man who knows who he is in God and has something to offer — not someone desperate to receive.
weeks.coreTension: Single men often have shallow friendships and pursue women from emptiness. This session offers a vision for both that flows from the identity work of the first five weeks.

teaching.title: I. Covenant Friendship — 1 Samuel 18:1–4

scriptures.text: "The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David...Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt."

prose: "The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David" — covenant-level connection, not casual friendship. Jonathan gave David his royal garments — an act of profound humility and sacrifice. What this models: friendship built on covenant, not convenience; involving sacrifice, not just enjoyment; holding under pressure.

teaching.title: II. Iron Sharpens Iron — Proverbs 27:17

scriptures.text: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another."

prose: Sharpening is not comfortable. A true friend is not someone who always agrees with you — he is someone who tells you the truth even when it costs him social comfort. The man who has no one like this is operating with a dull edge and doesn't know it.

teaching.title: III. Pursuing From Fullness — Not Yet Married

scriptures.text: "The man who is not yet satisfied in God will make an idol of the woman he pursues. He will ask her to be his savior, and she will fail — because only one Savior exists." — Segal

prose: From Not Yet Married, Segal identifies the core problem in how most men date: they pursue from emptiness. They are looking for someone to complete them, validate them, fill the void. The model from Boaz (Ruth 2–4): Protection → Provision → Intentionality → Decision.

teaching.title: IV. Do Not Defraud — 1 Thessalonians 4:3–6

scriptures.text: "That no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things."

prose: The word "wrong" (pleonektein) means to defraud — to take more than your share. Signs of defrauding in dating: physical escalation before commitment; letting her believe the relationship is more serious than you intend; "hanging out" indefinitely without clarity of intent. Passivity is not kindness. It is self-protection at her expense.

scriptureRefs.text: "The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David...Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt."
"Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another."
"That no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things."

discussionQuestions: Do you have a friend who would tell you a hard truth? When did he last do it? If not — what has kept that from developing?
Why do men drift into isolation in their 20s and 30s? What drives that in your own life specifically?
Segal distinguishes pursuing from emptiness vs. fullness. Which have you been operating from? What are the signs?
What does it mean to "defraud" someone in a dating relationship? What specific behaviors does that call out for you?
If the woman you have pursued or are pursuing looked at how you've done it — would she say you were clear, intentional, and honoring? Why or why not?
weeks.application:
If you are currently pursuing or interested in someone: Ask honestly — am I pursuing from fullness or emptiness? What is my actual foundation? Write it down.
If you are not currently pursuing anyone: Write down the 3 most important non-physical qualities you want in a future wife. What do those choices reveal about what you actually value?
reading: Not Yet Married — dating and pursuit chapters — Segal

weeks.title: Money, Calling & Mission
weeks.subtitle: Stewardship, Work as Worship & Investing the Freedoms of Singleness
weeks.bigIdea: How you handle money reveals what you trust. How you approach your work reveals what you worship. And the freedoms of singleness — time, mobility, undivided focus — are a stewardship responsibility, not just a perk to be consumed.
weeks.coreTension: Single men often either over-identify with work (using achievement to manage loneliness) or under-invest in it (waiting for life to "really start" when they get married). This session reframes both work and money as arenas of mission.

teaching.title: I. Work Was Given Before Sin — Genesis 2:15

scriptures.text: "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it."

prose: This command comes in Genesis 2 — before Genesis 3, before the fall. Work is not punishment. It is calling. The word work (abad) is etymologically linked to worship — work and worship share the same root. The word keep (shamar) means to guard, protect, preserve. Stewardship, not exploitation.

teaching.title: II. Working as for Christ — Colossians 3:23–24

scriptures.text: "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward."

prose: Paul wrote this to slaves — people with the least interesting, least fulfilling work imaginable. "Work heartily" — Greek psuche, literally "from the soul." What would it look like to treat your least favorite work task this week as if Jesus Himself were going to see it?

teaching.title: III. Two Masters — Matthew 6:24

scriptures.text: "No one can serve two masters...You cannot serve God and money."

prose: Jesus does not say you should not serve both. He says you cannot. One will always win. How do you know if money is your master? What do you most fear losing? What occupies the most mental energy? The borrower is slave to the lender (Proverbs 22:7) — debt decisions made in your 20s and 30s constrain your freedom for a decade.

teaching.title: IV. The Freedoms of Singleness Are a Stewardship — Not Yet Married
prose: Segal challenges single men with a question most have never been asked: "Are you investing the freedoms of singleness into something bigger than yourself, or just consuming them?"

The freedoms: Time — evenings and weekends belong to you in a way they will not once you have a spouse and family. Mobility — you can go where God calls without negotiating a family's needs. Financial margin — you are likely supporting only yourself. Focused attention — 1 Corinthians 7:32: "The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord." Undivided devotion is not a consolation prize. It is a strategic advantage.

scriptureRefs.text: "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it."
"Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward."
"No one can serve two masters...You cannot serve God and money."

discussionQuestions: Do you see your current work as meaningful? How does Colossians 3:23 change or confirm that?
If money is your master when you most fear losing it — what are you most afraid of losing financially, and what does that fear reveal?
Are you carrying debt? How does it affect your sense of freedom and options?
Segal asks: "Are you investing the freedoms of singleness into something bigger than yourself, or just consuming them?" How would you honestly answer that right now?
What would genuinely generous look like at your current income level — not someday, but this month?
weeks.application:
Pull up your last 30 days of bank and credit card transactions. Categorize your spending. Bring one honest observation to share next week. Not a plan, not a resolution. Just an observation.
Read Not Yet Married chapters on mission and purpose in singleness. Note one specific way you have been treating singleness as a holding pattern rather than a season of active investment.
reading: Not Yet Married — mission and purpose chapters — Segal

weeks.title: Anger, Entitlement & the Shadow Self
weeks.subtitle: The Male Blind Spots Most Groups Never Name
weeks.bigIdea: Every man has a shadow — the part of himself he has learned to suppress, deny, or redirect into something more socially acceptable. For men, the shadow most often takes the form of anger, entitlement, or passive control. These are not separate from the identity work of this series; they are what happens when "I am the beloved" is not yet believed in the places that matter most.
weeks.coreTension: Most men's groups go deep on sexuality but avoid anger and entitlement — which are often more destructive to relationships and more resistant to change. This session names what most groups skip, in the same spirit of grace that has marked this series from Week 1.
weeks.opening: Don't ease into this one. Ask directly: "When you are angry — really angry, not mildly frustrated — what do you do with it? Do you go loud, go cold, or disappear? Take a second to actually think about that." Give men 60 seconds of silence. Then share your own honest answer. Specifically. Not vague.

teaching.title: I. Be Angry and Do Not Sin — Ephesians 4:26–27

scriptures.text: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil."

prose: The command is not "don't be angry." It is "be angry and do not sin" — anger is assumed, even permitted, as a legitimate human emotion. The problem is not anger itself but what you do with it. "Give no opportunity to the devil" — unresolved anger is an open door. The longer it sits, the more territory it claims. Anger left unaddressed doesn't disappear; it calcifies.

teaching.title: II. Slow to Anger — James 1:19–20

scriptures.text: "Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God."

prose: "The anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" — this is not a prohibition on righteous anger, but it is a sharp check on self-righteous anger. Most of men's anger is not righteous indignation at injustice. It is pain, fear, or unmet expectation routed through a more socially acceptable channel. The question to ask when angry: What am I actually afraid of right now? The answer is almost always more honest than the anger itself.

teaching.title: III. Entitlement Disguised as Leadership — Matthew 20:20–28

scriptures.text: "Jesus called them to him and said, 'You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them...It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant.'"

prose: The sons of Zebedee wanted the best seats in the Kingdom — authority, status, recognition. Jesus doesn't shame their desire for greatness. He redirects it: the path to greatness is service, not position. Entitlement says "I deserve X." Service says "what does this person need?" For single men, entitlement in relationships often looks like: expecting women to respond to pursuit on your timeline, expecting brotherhood without investing in it, expecting spiritual growth without the disciplines.

teaching.title: IV. Passive Control — The Shadow Version of Leadership
prose: Men are often taught that aggression is bad. What is less often named is that passivity can be just as controlling. Passive control includes: going silent to make a point; withholding warmth until you get what you want; "checking out" emotionally when things get uncomfortable; letting a woman carry emotional labor because it's easier than engaging.

The connection back to Weeks 1–3: a man who has not found his belovedness in God is constantly managing a deficit. Anger, entitlement, and passive control are all management strategies for that deficit. When a man knows he is beloved — actually believes it — the urgency behind those strategies begins to dissolve. He no longer has to take by force or manipulation what the Father has already given freely.

scriptureRefs.text: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil."
"Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God."
"Jesus called them to him and said, 'You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them...It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant.'"

discussionQuestions: What does anger look like for you — do you go cold, go loud, or disappear? Which pattern do you use most?
When was the last time you were genuinely angry? What was underneath it — what were you actually afraid of or feeling?
Have you ever used passivity as a form of control — going silent, withholding, checking out to make a point? Be honest.
What do you feel entitled to in relationships — friendships, women you've dated, or this group — that you haven't named out loud?
Jesus had righteous anger (Matthew 21:12) and also controlled it (Matthew 26:52). What is the difference between his anger and the anger you tend to carry?
weeks.application:
This week, when you feel anger before you act on it, pause and write: "What am I actually afraid of right now?" You don't have to resolve it. Just name it.
Bring one honest observation about your anger or entitlement pattern to share next week. Not a plan for fixing it — an observation. What have you noticed?
reading: Not Yet Married — character formation chapters — Segal
Abba's Child Ch. 2 — re-read with the shadow self in mind — Manning

weeks.title: Failure, Grace & Forward
weeks.subtitle: Peter's Restoration, No Condemnation & The Beloved Man on Mission
weeks.bigIdea: God does not disqualify men who fail — He restores them and sends them back out. The most devastating failures in your life do not have the final word. And the man who has been loved by God, dismantled his Impostor, fought his battles honestly, and invested the freedoms of his singleness is not waiting to begin his life — he is already living it.
weeks.coreTension: Many men carry shame from past sin that has convinced them they are disqualified from being fully used by God. This session names that lie directly and points to the most powerful restoration story in Scripture.

teaching.title: I. The Fall — Luke 22:54–62

scriptures.text: "And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord...And he went out and wept bitterly."

prose: Context: Peter had followed Jesus for three years. He declared "You are the Christ." He witnessed the Transfiguration. He promised at the Last Supper he would never abandon Jesus. Hours later, he denied knowing Jesus three times to a servant girl by a fire.

Jesus was being led to his death. He turned. He made eye contact. That look broke Peter. This was not a small moral failing — it was public, repeated betrayal of his closest friend during his greatest hour of need. And this is the man who would preach the first sermon at Pentecost.

teaching.title: II. The Restoration — John 21:15–19

scriptures.text: "When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, 'Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?'...He said to him, 'Feed my lambs.'"

prose: Three denials. Three restorations. Jesus is not accidental with the number. He does not open the conversation by listing Peter's failures or requiring a probationary period. He asks: Do you love me? And then he commissions him immediately: Feed my lambs. Tend my sheep. Feed my sheep.

teaching.title: III. No Condemnation — Right Now — Romans 8:1

scriptures.text: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."

prose: Now — not after sufficient suffering, not after adequate penance. Right now, in your current state of failure or struggle. No condemnation — not less condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. None. The condition is not moral performance. It is union with Christ.

teaching.title: IV. Shame vs. Godly Sorrow

scriptures.text: "Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death."

prose: Shame says: I am bad. I am what I did. This defines me. I need to hide. Inward-focused. Leads to hiding, isolation, and performance. The Impostor feeds on shame — it gives him something to manage.
Godly sorrow says: I did something wrong. It grieved God and hurt others. I need to repent and be restored. Outward-focused. Leads to repentance and restoration. Godly sorrow is a gift.

teaching.title: V. Pressing On — Philippians 3:12–14

scriptures.text: "Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on...forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus."

prose: Paul wrote this near the end of his life and still said: I have not arrived. Press on. "Forgetting what lies behind" — in both directions. Not dwelling on failures. Not coasting on past successes. The upward call is present and ongoing. Not waiting for marriage. Not contingent on someone choosing you. Right now. Press on.

scriptureRefs.text: "And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord...And he went out and wept bitterly."
"When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, 'Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?'...He said to him, 'Feed my lambs.'"
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
"Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death."

"Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on...forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus."

discussionQuestions: Is there something you have done that you have told yourself — even quietly — disqualifies you from being fully used by God? What would it mean if that belief is a lie?
Jesus restored Peter publicly and completely — no probation, no list of conditions. What is your honest reaction to that kind of grace?
What is the difference between shame and godly sorrow in your own experience? Which do you tend to live in after you fail?
What is the single most significant thing from these nine weeks that has shifted something in you?
Segal says the man who finds his identity in God's love — not in being chosen by a woman — is free. What would that freedom actually look like for you in the next 12 months?
weeks.application: Begin drafting your letter. Write to yourself — where you want to be in one year spiritually, relationally, and practically. You will seal it next week in the final session. Be specific. Not "I want to grow" — what does growth actually look like, measured?
reading: Not Yet Married — final chapters — Segal

weeks.title: Vision, Legacy & Multiplying Forward
weeks.subtitle: The Commission — Passing On What You've Received
weeks.bigIdea: The end of this series is not the end of the work — it is the beginning of passing it on. The beloved man on mission is not a consumer of good content; he is a multiplier. The question is not whether you are ready. The question is whether you are willing.
weeks.coreTension: Men often receive well but struggle to transmit. This final session takes everything from the previous nine weeks and asks the hardest question: who is one man in your life who needs what you received in this room — and what are you going to do about it?
weeks.opening: Before any teaching, go around the room: "What is one thing from the last 10 weeks that has genuinely changed something in you — not just what you know, but how you actually live? One sentence. Be specific." Go all the way around. Do not rush this. It is the most important moment of Week 10.

teaching.title: I. Entrust to Faithful Men — 2 Timothy 2:2

scriptures.text: "What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also."

prose: Paul's model of discipleship is not a one-to-many broadcast — it is a one-to-few transmission: Paul → Timothy → faithful men → others. Four generations in one verse. The man who receives something from God and does not pass it on has received it for himself only. The man who passes it on multiplies what he received beyond anything he could produce alone.
You are not being asked to be a pastor or expert. You are being asked to be a faithful man — someone who walks with another man in the same direction you have been walking for 10 weeks.

teaching.title: II. Sent — John 17:18

scriptures.text: "As you sent me into the world, I have sent them into the world."

prose: Jesus' prayer in John 17 is not a retirement speech. It is a commissioning. The pattern: the Father sends the Son; the Son sends the disciples; the disciples send others. You are inside this pattern right now. The belovedness you have been receiving in this room is not meant to stay in this room. It is meant to move through you into someone else's life.

teaching.title: III. The Commission Is Already Active — Matthew 28:19–20

scriptures.text: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations...teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."

prose: "Go" is a present participle in the Greek — as you are going. Not: "when you have fully arrived, then go." As you are going — in your current state, with your current wounds and incomplete formation — make disciples. The commission does not wait for you to be ready. It begins now. And the promise that closes it: I am with you always. The same presence that has been at work in this room for 10 weeks goes with you when you leave it.

teaching.title: IV. The Beloved Man Multiplied — Closing Vision

scriptures.text: "Define yourself radically as one beloved by God. This is the true self. Every other identity is illusion." — Brennan Manning

prose: What would it look like if every man in this room went and walked with one other man — one man who is where you were 10 weeks ago? Not a program. Not a curriculum necessarily. Just one man showing up consistently for another man. Over 10 weeks, asking the hard questions. Going first. Naming the real thing.

The man who knows he is beloved is free to give without demanding in return. Free to invest in another man without needing credit for it. Free to pass on what was given to him — because he is not holding on to it for survival. He received it as a gift. He gives it as a gift. That is the beloved man on mission.

scriptureRefs.text: "What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also."
"As you sent me into the world, I have sent them into the world."
"Go therefore and make disciples of all nations...teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."

discussionQuestions: Who is one man in your life right now who is where you were 10 weeks ago? What would it look like to specifically invest in him — not in general, but this month?
What from this series has genuinely changed how you think — not just what you know, but how you actually live day-to-day?
Segal: "The man satisfied in God is free." Are you freer than you were 10 weeks ago? In what specific way?
What does "multiplying forward" look like for you — in your friendships, your faith, your work, and your singleness?
What is one commitment you are making tonight — not to this group, but to God — about how you will live the next 12 months?
weeks.application: Father, thank you for these men. For every honest conversation, every hard question, every moment of vulnerability in this room. We ask that what you started here you continue to completion. That these men would know — not just believe — that they are loved by you. That they would not wait to begin their lives. That they would pursue with integrity, fight their battles honestly, invest their singleness with intention, and know that when they fail, you restore them and send them back out. Remind them, whenever they forget, that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. And remind them that they are the beloved. Amen.
reading: Not Yet Married — closing chapters on mission and purpose — Segal
